title: Staged restoration schedule and customer quiet-window templates (2026)
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Overview:

This document describes Redwood's staged restoration approach for multi-service incidents, the associated quiet-window practice for customer communications, and reusable status page and customer templates. It codifies responsibilities, timing windows, verification gates, and escalation thresholds to reduce noisy updates during large recoveries while preserving transparency and compliance.

Goals:
- Restore customer-facing functionality in prioritized stages with safety gates.
- Reduce customer confusion and churn by consolidating updates into structured quiet windows.
- Provide ready-to-send status and email templates to minimize drafting time during incidents.
- Ensure on-call teams have clear verification checklists and rollback criteria.

Applicability:
This playbook applies to incidents impacting Redwood-hosted inference endpoints, console availability, or billing/usage reporting services. Use for partial or full degradations where staggered restoration reduces blast radius.

Key roles and responsibilities:
1) Primary on-call (Responder): initial triage, mitigation, and first updates.
2) Secondary (Support): service-level mitigation and cross-team coordination.
3) Incident Commander (IC): orchestrates staged restoration schedule, approves quiet windows, makes go/no-go decisions.
4) Communications owner: drafts status and customer emails using templates below.

SLO and threshold triggers for staged restoration:
- Error rate > 5% for > 3 minutes on critical route -> urgent incident (stage 0).
- Median latency > 750ms for > 10 minutes -> consider partial throttling and stage-based recovery.
- Token processing backlog > 10 minutes average -> trigger cache warmup and staged capacity increase.

Staged restoration phases (recommended cadence):
Phase 0 — Containment (0–20 minutes):
- Reduce blast radius: disable autoscaling policies that exacerbate thrash, apply circuit breakers per service.
- Short customer notice: initial status posted (see template A).
- IC assignment mandatory.

Phase 1 — Stabilize core control plane (20–60 minutes):
- Restore control-plane APIs and monitoring; ensure events are flowing.
- Verify internal health checks: 
  - kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l app=<service> --field-selector=status.phase=Running
  - curl -sS https://internal-health/<service>/live | grep OK
- If checks fail, remain in containment and escalate to platform infra.

Phase 2 — Gradual customer traffic re-introduction (60–180 minutes):
- Reopen traffic for low-priority routes or small customer cohorts (canary groups).
- Monitor KPIs for 3x the usual check interval before widening.
- Execute cache/KV warmups and pre-populate common prompt prefixes where applicable.

Phase 3 — Bulk restore + verification (3–12 hours):
- Progressive scaling to full capacity with automated throttling fallback.
- Run synthetic workload sweep: 50 requests/min across top 100 prompt templates.
- Confirm error rate below 1% and P95 latency within SLOs before marking restored.

Phase 4 — Closure and follow-up (>12 hours):
- Publish final status and postmortem timeline.
- Coordinate with Customer Success for high-touch outreach.

Quiet-window practice (purpose and cadence):
- Definition: A quiet window is a pre-approved time window during active restoration where customer-facing updates are batched to reduce churn and confusion.
- Typical cadence: IC approves quiet windows of 30–90 minutes during phases 1–3.
- When to use: multi-service rollouts, cascading capacity throttles, or when frequent partial changes would create contradictory messages.
- Exceptions: security incidents, legal/regulatory impacts, or new PII exposures always require immediate notification.

Quiet-window rules:
- Communications owner posts an initial notice that updates will be provided at fixed intervals (e.g., every 60 minutes) and lists the next expected update time.
- Emergency channel (internal Slack #incident-critical) remains open for internal stakeholders and affected large customers.
- If situation materially changes (customer data exposure, full outage of SLA-bound service), quiet window is lifted and immediate update sent.

Status page messages (components):
- Title line: short and factual (e.g., "Degraded: Inference API elevated error rate").
- Affected services: list with product-impact tags (API, Console, Billing).
- Impact: brief customer-facing description and user-facing symptoms.
- Current status: staging phase and expected next update time.
- Actions underway: short bullet points of mitigation.
- Owner and contact: names and ‘urgent’ contact link or email.

Template A — Initial status page (short):
- Title: "Investigating: Increased error rate for /v1/generate"
- Body: "We are aware of elevated error rates for text generation requests. Our on-call team is actively investigating. We'll post updates every 60 minutes or sooner if there is a material change."
- Next update: ISO timestamp

Template B — Quiet-window update (scheduled):
- Title: "Monitoring: Partial recovery in canary cohort"
- Body: "We have reintroduced a fraction of traffic to a small cohort and are monitoring key metrics (error rate, P95 latency). No action required from customers. Next scheduled update in 60 minutes."

Template C — Customer email (high-touch):
- Subject: "Redwood incident update — [short description] — ongoing"
- Greeting: "Hello <CustomerName>,\nOur engineering team is currently restoring service for <affected feature>. We understand the impact and are prioritizing your traffic. The next planned update is at <time>. For questions, reply to this message and your account team will respond."

Verification checklist (pre-announce stage completion):
- Synthetic test sweep: all 200-sample requests return successful status.
- Telemetry sanity: error rate < 1% for 30 minutes, P95 latency within SLO.
- KV/Cache warm: tail-latency stable and cache-hit rate > 85%.
- Billing/usage reporting validated for delayed batches.

Rollback / abort criteria during staged rollouts:
- Any major customer cohort reports repeated errors > 3 occurrences in 10 minutes.
- Error rate doubles or P95 increases > 50% relative to baseline during widening.
- Unrecoverable dependencies fail health checks.

Game day and training guidance:
- Run an annual staged-restoration game day with a simulated cross-region capacity loss. Include communications drills for quiet-window templates.
- Success metrics: time to first canary traffic (< 90 minutes), mean time to full restore (target < 6 hours), and correctness of status messaging (peer-reviewed).

Post-incident actions and postmortem checklist:
1) Record timeline with exact timestamps for each phase change.
2) Assign action owners and target remediation dates.
3) Include communications audit: what updates were sent and to which customers.
4) Retrospective game-day to validate changes if remediation impacts operational playbook.

Related links and references:
- Link: internal runbook index (search: "staged restore").
- Link: incident-comm-templates collection.

Appendix: quick health-check commands and samples:
- Check core pods: kubectl get pods -n inference -l tier=backend
- Perform a synthetic generation: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"prompt":"hello"}'
- Verify queue depth: curl -s https://internal-metrics/queues | jq '.inference_queue.depth'
